reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ATS-ERS
clinicalPearls: A recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax that occurs in temporal relation to menstruation, typically within a day or two around the onset of menses
It is the most common manifestation of the thoracic endometriosis syndrome and characteristically affects the right hemithorax
Should be suspected in a woman of reproductive age with recurrent right-sided pneumothoraces linked to her menstrual cycle
Many patients have coexisting pelvic endometriosis, and the condition may present alongside catamenial haemothorax or haemoptysis
Diaphragmatic defects (fenestrations) and endometrial implants on the diaphragm or pleura are frequently found at surgery
Diagnosis rests on the cyclical clinical history supported by CT and confirmed at video-assisted thoracoscopy with inspection of the diaphragm and pleura
Management combines surgical repair of diaphragmatic defects and resection of implants with hormonal suppression of ovulation to reduce recurrence
Pleurodesis may be added to lower the risk of further pneumothoraces
reference.pathophysiology: Catamenial pneumothorax is linked to thoracic endometriosis, in which endometrial-type tissue reaches the thorax, thought to occur through diaphragmatic fenestrations, transdiaphragmatic passage of air and cells from the peritoneal cavity, or microembolisation. Cyclical hormonal stimulation causes these ectopic implants and the associated diaphragmatic defects to change with menstruation, allowing air to enter the pleural space around menses. Prostaglandin-mediated effects at menstruation and shedding of implants may further contribute. The right-sided predominance is attributed to the pattern of peritoneal fluid circulation directing material to the right diaphragm.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax from cystic lung disease such as lymphangioleiomyomatosis
Recurrent pneumothorax from bullous or emphysematous disease
Catamenial haemoptysis or haemothorax from thoracic endometriosis
additionalInvestigations: Careful menstrual and gynaecological history correlating events with the cycle
Chest imaging including CT to characterise pneumothorax and any diaphragmatic or pleural abnormality
Video-assisted thoracoscopic inspection of the diaphragm and pleura for defects and implants
Histological confirmation of endometrial tissue where lesions are resected
Gynaecological assessment for coexisting pelvic endometriosis
redFlags: Tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise requiring emergency decompression
Large or bilateral pneumothorax causing significant respiratory distress
Associated catamenial haemothorax with significant blood loss
Frequent recurrences despite treatment indicating need for definitive surgery
reference.prognosis: With combined surgical repair and hormonal suppression outcomes are generally good, but recurrence rates are appreciable if either component is omitted, so multidisciplinary follow-up is important.
pitfalls: Not eliciting the cyclical timing and treating episodes as ordinary spontaneous pneumothorax
Managing with a chest drain alone without addressing the underlying diaphragmatic defects and implants
Omitting hormonal suppression after surgery and allowing recurrence
Failing to assess for coexisting pelvic endometriosis
